content: The training of healthcare workers in managing intrapartum emergency obstetric care is critical for improving maternal and neonatal outcomes. Accurate coding of death certificates is essential for understanding the causes of perinatal mortality. A trained coder applies ICD-10 rules to assign specific codes to the conditions listed on the death certificate. For example, massive pulmonary hemorrhage originating in the perinatal period is coded as P26. The main perinatal cause of death, recorded on line (a) of the perinatal death certificate or line (d) of the WHO death certificate, must be coded within the ranges P05–P96 (perinatal conditions) or Q00–Q99 (congenital anomalies). Exceptions exist, such as neonatal tetanus, which is always coded as A33. The assignment of conditions follows ICD-10 Volume 2 rules for perinatal mortality coding. The underlying cause of death is defined as the disease or condition initiating the chain of events leading to death. This cause should be as specific as possible. Maternal diseases or conditions affecting the fetus or infant are coded similarly to perinatal causes of death, using codes for maternal factors and complications of pregnancy, labor, and delivery. These codes must also be used for any other maternal conditions captured. The ICD-PM (International Classification of Diseases for Perinatal Mortality) framework classifies perinatal deaths based on timing: antepartum (A), intrapartum (I), or neonatal (N). This classification provides valuable information for analyzing and targeting interventions. Antepartum causes are designated with an A, intrapartum causes with an I, and neonatal causes with an N. ICD-10 codes have been reorganized to better represent pathologies at different times of perinatal death, excluding codes not considered causes of perinatal death. Growth restriction is a significant challenge to detect, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, due to limited resources such as ultrasound and accurate pregnancy dating. Even in high-income settings, growth restriction may be a consequence of underlying pathology rather than the primary cause of perinatal death. The distinction between causality and consequence is often unclear. Growth-restricted fetuses are at high risk for adverse outcomes, including perinatal mortality, and may be under-recognized contributors to global perinatal mortality. Assessing growth for gestational age is recommended for all fetuses to better understand the role of growth restriction in perinatal deaths. Prematurity is a major contributor to perinatal mortality. It is important to distinguish idiopathic preterm labor from preterm delivery due to pathology or provider-initiated interventions. Prematurity should not be listed as the main cause of death unless it is the only known condition. Low birth weight and prematurity are coded together in ICD-10, but their relationship is not always reciprocal. Prematurity should only be accepted as the main condition if supported by evidence, such as a gestational age of less than 28 weeks. Obstructed labor is a critical condition that can lead to perinatal death. It may initiate a sequence of events resulting in death or be caused by a preceding condition, such as a contracted maternal pelvis or fetal malpresentation. Preventing obstructed labor or ensuring prompt access to emergency obstetric care is essential. If obstructed labor is the starting point of a sequence leading to perinatal death, it should be recorded as the main maternal condition. HIV and AIDS are often over-attributed as causes of death in individuals known to have these conditions. It is important to carefully evaluate and document the actual cause of death to avoid misclassification.
